keyVerseText: Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place; Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite: for they had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him.
rootMeaning: The name צוֹפַר (Tsôwphar) derives from the root צָפַר (tsâphar), which primarily means 'to depart early' or 'to go early.' This etymology suggests a sense of promptness or early departure, possibly implying swiftness or readiness to move. While the root's meaning is somewhat uncertain, the literal sense of 'departing early' adds a dynamic nuance beyond the simple personal name, hinting at movement or transition that may metaphorically relate to the character's role or disposition.
usageInScripture: The word צוֹפַר (Tsôwphar) appears four times in Scripture, consistently referring to the same individual: the third friend of Job. It is translated mainly as 'Zophar' or 'and Zophar,' showing a stable usage as a proper name rather than a common noun. This consistency underscores the importance of this character in the narrative of Job, emphasizing his identity and role as one of Job's companions who come to comfort and challenge him.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding צוֹפַר as meaning 'departing early' enriches our comprehension of this figure within the book of Job and the broader biblical narrative. Zophar, as one of Job's friends, represents a voice that arrives promptly to engage with suffering and theological questioning. This name reminds believers that God's providence includes timely interventions, even through human agents who may challenge us. Reflecting on Zophar's role encourages faith in God's sovereign orchestration of relationships and trials, pointing ultimately to Christ's compassion and wisdom in the midst of human suffering.
keyVerseReflection: In Job 2:11, the verse states that 'Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite' came together to mourn and comfort Job after his calamities. The inclusion of Zophar by name highlights his presence as one of the appointed friends who respond to Job's distress. The name's meaning, connected to 'departing early,' may subtly emphasize the readiness of these friends to come quickly to Job’s side, underscoring the biblical theme of fellowship and support in times of trial.
